criteria.note: The TL;DR answers 'how do I eat safely in Korea' in the first 200 words, but the piece explicitly repositions itself away from the celiac intent behind the keyword and validates its recommendations only for NCGS.
criteria.evidence_quote: Everything we recommend works for NCGS.

criteria.note: Description is on-length and carries the keyword, but the title runs ~76 characters before the render-time ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix pushes it near 96, and 'celiac' is absent from it.
criteria.evidence_quote: The Real Gluten-Free Guide to Korea: A Couple's Field-Tested Handbook (2026)

criteria.note: Headings state claims rather than label sections, and the Tier 1/Tier 2 sub-structure means a skim of headings alone reproduces the argument.
Six-plus internal links, each placed at the point where a reader would want the deeper post (phrases, labels, BBQ, bakeries), not stuffed.
All five Q/As are reproduced visibly in the body and each stands alone as a rich result; only trivial wording drift between frontmatter and visible text.
Named dishes ordered, a phone call to franchise HQ, a bakery owner's 90/10 admission, a product silently renamed online, and the pink-vs-green package detail are all observed specifics.
Korean terms are given with hangul plus romanisation, and product/brand names and ratios are precise enough to verify on a shelf.
Attribution exists but is entirely first-person and unlinked (a call to HQ, an owner conversation, a GFCO claim); the regulatory labelling claims carry no source or date at all.
criteria.evidence_quote: Barley (보리) and rye (호밀) are not mandatory allergen declarations

criteria.note: The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish (NCGS vs celiac, unverified menu items, per-branch contamination) and contains no undisclosed commercial links.

findings.quote: The Real Gluten-Free Guide to Korea: A Couple's Field-Tested Handbook (2026)
findings.why: At ~76 characters the title already exceeds the 60-character budget, and layout.js appends ' | Gluten-Free Korea' at render time, taking it to roughly 96 — the tail will truncate in SERPs. The target keyword's distinguishing word, 'celiac', is also missing from the title entirely.
findings.fix: Retitle to something like 'Celiac Travel in Korea: A Field-Tested Guide' (43 chars + suffix = 63) or shorter, so the keyword survives truncation and the appended brand string still fits.

findings.quote: Barley (보리) and rye (호밀) are not mandatory allergen declarations
findings.why: This is the single most consequential regulatory claim in the piece for a celiac reader, and it carries no attribution — no link to the MFDS labelling standard, no publication or revision date. The same applies to the '22 flagged allergens' figure and the GFCO certification claim for 237 Pizza.
findings.fix: Link the MFDS (식약처) allergen labelling notice with its revision date, and link 237 Pizza's GFCO certification listing with the certification date.

findings.quote: Everything we recommend works for NCGS.
findings.why: The frontmatter keyword is 'celiac travel korea', but the article's core evidence base is explicitly non-celiac. Celiac searchers arriving on this page get honest caveats rather than celiac-validated vetting, which risks pogo-sticking back to the SERP.
findings.fix: Add a short 'If you're celiac, start here' block near the top that consolidates the celiac-specific rules already scattered through the piece (shared grill, shared fryer, barley in the ingredient list, call-ahead script), so the celiac intent is served in one place.

findings.quote: Only commit to dedicated GF bakeries like monil2 house and Cafe Rebirth.
findings.why: The frontmatter answer and the visible body answer differ ('and Cafe Rebirth' vs 'Cafe Rebirth, and similar. Full list in our...'). Google requires FAQ markup to match visible content; drift like this can invalidate the rich result.
findings.fix: Sync the frontmatter FAQ strings to the visible body text verbatim, minus link markup, and add a build-time check that diffs the two.

findings.quote: I called the franchise headquarters directly to confirm
findings.why: A useful primary check, but with no date it cannot be revalidated — franchise recipes and suppliers change, and a reader in 2027 has no way to judge staleness.
findings.fix: Add the month and year of the call, e.g. 'I called the franchise headquarters in March 2026 to confirm', and do the same for the bakery flour-ratio conversation.

criteria.note: The piece is generally honest about being experience-based, but several product-level, safety-relevant claims (specific snack SKUs, chip flavours, Korea's labelling law, a percentage range for 'rice bread') are stated flatly with no source and no explicit marking as the authors' own check.
criteria.evidence_quote: Chamsal Seolbyeong (참쌀설병) in the **pink** package is safe. The green package contains wheat.

criteria.note: Products, neighbourhoods and dates are checkable and internally consistent, but one figure is presented as a general fact when the only supporting evidence in the text is a single anecdote about a 90/10 blend.
criteria.evidence_quote: Many "rice bread" shops blend 10-30% wheat flour into the dough.

criteria.note: The article repeatedly states how it knows (personal visits, label reading, a direct call to ssaltongdak HQ) and what that method cannot establish ("we haven't personally verified it", "fine for her", branch-level cross-contamination), and never dresses label scanning up as ingredient analysis.

Framing is unusually careful overall — NCGS vs celiac is stated up front, shared grills and shared facilities are flagged — but one packaged product is declared flatly "safe" with no re-verify caveat and no shared-facility note, which is an absolute safety claim label reading cannot support.
criteria.evidence_quote: Chamsal Seolbyeong (참쌀설병) in the **pink** package is safe. The green package contains wheat.

criteria.note: The piece carries an explicit last-updated date and tells readers to re-check packets, but the product- and label-level claims are undated and the article never states that Korean manufacturers reformulate without notice, so a four-month-old snack list reads as current.
criteria.evidence_quote: Last updated: April 2026. Every restaurant listed has been personally visited by me and my wife.

criteria.note: Korean terms, the 알레르기 유발물질 line, the 22-item allergen count, and the load-bearing fact that mandatory allergen labelling covers wheat only — with barley and rye excluded — are all stated correctly and acted on.

The reader gets a copyable Korean allergy phrase, a reconfirmation script, the exact hangul strings to scan for, an explicit instruction to read the ingredient list rather than the packaging headline, and a route to confirm at the branch level.

findings.quote: Chamsal Seolbyeong (참쌀설병) in the **pink** package is safe. The green package contains wheat.
findings.why: This is the only unhedged absolute safety verdict in the piece. It sits in a bullet that, unlike the chips bullet beneath it, carries no "re-verify on the actual packet" caveat and no shared-facility note. A celiac reader could buy the pink package on the article's word alone, when what the authors can actually have established is that the label listed no wheat on the day they read it. It falls short of blocking only because the surrounding section teaches the reader to scan labels themselves and explicitly tells celiacs the allergen line is insufficient.
findings.fix: Rewrite as observation plus limit, e.g. "the pink 참쌀설병 has read clean for us; the green package lists wheat. Re-check the ingredient line each time, and note that neither carries a dedicated-facility claim."

findings.quote: **A handful of chips that usually pass** — Poca Chip Original (NOT onion flavor), Doritos cheese (NOT other flavors), Banana Kick, Yegam (all flavors), plain corn chips.
findings.why: Six named SKUs with flavour-level carve-outs are safety-relevant claims a reader will act on in a shop, yet the basis is never stated — label read, manufacturer contact, or accumulated habit. "Yegam (all flavors)" is the broadest claim and the least supported. The trailing "Always re-verify" mitigates but does not source it.
findings.fix: State the basis and date for the list ("allergen lines read in-store, spring 2026"), and narrow blanket claims like "all flavors" to the specific variants actually checked.

findings.quote: Many "rice bread" shops blend 10-30% wheat flour into the dough.
findings.why: A numeric range presented as an industry pattern, while the only evidence offered anywhere in the article is one owner quoting 10%. The upper bound of 30% has no visible origin, which is the kind of specific-sounding figure this criterion exists to catch.
findings.fix: Either attribute the range ("the shops we've asked have quoted us between 10% and 30%") or drop to the figure actually witnessed.

findings.quote: Last updated: April 2026. Every restaurant listed has been personally visited by me and my wife.
findings.why: The article is dated, but the packaged-food claims — the snack list, the tamari availability by retailer, the ssaltongdak headquarters answer — carry no verification date of their own and no warning that Korean manufacturers reformulate silently. Read four months on, an undated snack list presents as current.
findings.fix: Date the perishable claims individually ("HQ confirmed by phone, March 2026") and add one line stating that Korean formulations change without notice, so any product claim older than a few months must be re-read at the shelf.
